The trap is that the project director's account is backed by two documents (the November progress report and the consultant's claim), while the opposing account comes from the owner, who is also interested. C9 is the only item that settles H2 and R3: it shows response times measured from submission, the drafts held by the contractor, and the structural RFI dates. case.title: Corran Valley Medical Centre: a 26-week slip and a claim due on 1 December
case.setting: Callerby Construct is a regional general contractor. It built Corran Valley Medical Centre, a four-storey steel-frame medical building, for the developer Halden Medical Properties under a £14.6m contract. The contract completion date was 30 April 2026. Practical completion came on 29 October 2026. Halden is deducting liquidated damages. Callerby's project director and a claims consultant have drafted a claim that blames the delay on Halden. Halden blames Callerby. The project's lender appointed an independent monitoring surveyor, and the project ran its information requests (RFIs) through a shared platform hosted by a third party. Callerby's Northern region also delivered Kestrel, a distribution warehouse, over the same period.
case.presentingRequest: Callerby's chief executive wants to know what actually caused the Corran Valley slip, and what Callerby should do about the drafted extension-of-time and prolongation claim, which is due to go to Halden on 1 December. She also wants to know what should happen inside the company.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Ruth Abernethy, chief executive, Callerby Construct, 12 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: 'Corran Valley Medical Centre reached practical completion on 29 October, 26 weeks after the contract date of 30 April. Halden is withholding £1.17m in liquidated damages. Our extension-of-time and prolongation claim for £1.9m is due to go to Halden on 1 December. Gareth says the slip is down to Halden's design changes and their architect's slow answers; Halden says the opposite. Before I sign anything I need to know what actually drove the slip and what we do next. On a brighter note, the Northern region had a good year: Kestrel warehouse handed over seven weeks early in March, and the regional early-handover incentive paid out to Colm Faraday's team.'

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Gareth Imrie, project director, 4 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: Says Halden 'redesigned the building while we were building it'. Cites six change orders, CO-07 to CO-12, including CO-09, which moved the MRI suite to level 2. Halden flagged it in September and it needed extra steel. 'We couldn't carry on with the frame until CO-09 was resolved, and the architect sat on our steel connection queries for weeks.' Confirms the tower crane went to the Kestrel job in October: 'Kestrel's hired crane failed its thorough examination, the region needed one, and ours was standing idle anyway. Colm and I agreed it.' Says he has 'had a word' with the site superintendent about 'chatting to Halden's clerk of works'.

initialEvidence.source: Draft claim summary, Fenmore Claims Advisory, prepared for Callerby, 28 Oct 2026
initialEvidence.text: The time impact analysis attributes the full 26-week delay to employer risk events: (a) owner change orders CO-07 to CO-12, issued 12 Sep–9 Dec 2025 and holding the structural frame: 17 weeks; (b) late information: 41 of 64 RFIs, including structural connection queries, open longer than the contractual response period: a further 9 weeks. RFI durations come from the 'created' date in the project RFI log. Programme inputs are the contractor's monthly updates. Claimed: a 26-week extension of time and £1.9m in prolongation costs. Engagement terms: Fenmore's fee includes 6% of sums recovered.

initialEvidence.source: Letter, Priya Varma, development manager, Halden Medical Properties, to Callerby, 10 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: 'We understand a delay claim is being prepared, so please note our position now. Your tower crane left site in October 2025 and did not come back until April. Your own superintendent told our clerk of works it had gone to another of your jobs. Our architect answered your queries promptly. The change orders concerned interior layouts and were small.' Halden will deduct liquidated damages in full and reserves its right to recover its own extra consultant and finance costs from Callerby.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Dale Pruitt, site superintendent, 5 Nov 2026
initialEvidence.text: 'Autumn and winter were dead. The crane and the frame gang went over to Kestrel and we did bits: drainage, level 1 blockwork.' Asked why: 'Above my pay grade. Gareth and Colm sorted it.' Asked whether levels 3–4 could have gone up: 'Steel was on the ground. Whether every connection query was answered, I couldn't swear to; that's Gareth's side.' Recalls that steel deliveries for levels 1–2 were 'all over the place in the summer'. Confirms he told Halden's clerk of works where the crane had gone: 'He asked. I wasn't going to lie.'

initialEvidence.source: Callerby monthly progress report no. 14 to Halden, November 2025, signed G. Imrie
initialEvidence.text: 'Frame: level 3–4 erection resequenced pending resolution of CO-09 structural information and outstanding connection queries. Tower crane temporarily demobilised to reduce standing costs during the design hold.' The programme update moves frame completion from 19 Dec 2025 to 'TBC – subject to CO-09'. Stated critical path: CO-09 design → frame → envelope → fit-out. The report does not yet claim any change to the contract completion date.

catalogue.title: Shared RFI platform export with audit timestamps, all project RFIs
catalogue.source: Project RFI platform, hosted by an independent software provider
catalogue.text: Users cannot edit the platform's audit trail. All 64 RFIs are included, each with 'created' (contractor draft opened), 'submitted' and 'answered' timestamps. Measured from submission, the architect's median response was 4 working days, and 62 of 64 were answered within the 10-working-day contract period. The two exceptions are RFI-052 (12 days) and RFI-058 (11 days), both on level 2 ceiling finishes in May 2026; the contractor marked both 'no programme impact' when submitting. Of the 41 RFIs the draft claim lists as late, 39 sat in contractor draft status for 9–47 days before submission. Structural RFIs, Oct 2025–Apr 2026: RFI-029 (submitted 2 Oct, answered 7 Oct), RFI-031 on CO-09 connections (10 Nov, 14 Nov), RFI-036 (28 Jan, 30 Jan).

catalogue.text: Handover on 13 Mar 2026, seven weeks ahead of contract. The client paid no early-completion bonus. The regional early-handover incentive was triggered for the Northern region team. Lessons learned: 'secure backup crane options at tender stage.'

Late responses from the owner's architect to the contractor's information requests held up critical-path work.
The contractor's redeployment of its own equipment or crews to other work held up critical-path work.
Late delivery of structural steel by the fabricator held up critical-path work.

actions.text: Submit the drafted 26-week extension-of-time and prolongation claim to Halden on 1 December as drafted.
Withdraw the drafted claim and settle the final account with Halden on the basis that the frame stoppage was Callerby's own responsibility.
Suspend the regional early-handover incentive scheme on the grounds that it drove the crane transfer.
Commission a second claims consultant to prepare an independent forensic delay analysis before deciding whether to submit any claim.
Issue the site superintendent a formal written warning for discussing the crane's whereabouts with Halden's clerk of works.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: By mid-October 2025 the Corran Valley frame was on programme. Steel for levels 3–4 had been delivered and stored on site, and erection was programmed to start on 21 October. Kestrel's hired crane had just failed its examination, and the project director and the regional director agreed to move Corran's tower crane TC-3 to Kestrel. It was dismantled on 20–22 October. The frame then stood idle for about 24 weeks, until the crane was re-erected in early April 2026, and the cladding subcontractor's lost slot added the knock-on time to a 26-week completion slip. The owner's change order CO-09 was issued after the crane had gone. It added only four level 2 infill beams, which were installed with a hired mobile crane by 12 December. The other change orders were fit-out work within float. Every structural RFI was answered within five working days. The draft claim's '41 late RFIs' comes from measuring from the date each draft was created, when 39 of them sat unsubmitted in the contractor's own draft status. The project director's November progress report blamed a 'design hold' and gave a different reason for removing the crane than the one recorded at the time by the lender's independent monitor, whose reports Callerby never disputed. The project director, the owner and the claims consultant (paid partly on recovery) are all interested parties. The independent monitor and the third-party platform's audit trail settle the dispute. Whether the regional incentive motivated the crane move cannot be established: it coincides with the move, but so does a real operational need at Kestrel.

answers.rationale: C4 is a contemporaneous independent record that Callerby never disputed. It shows the tower crane removed on 20–22 Oct, before CO-09 was issued on 6 Nov, with erection programmed to start on 21 Oct and the steel on site. CO-09 affected only four level 2 infill beams, which were installed by 12 Dec while levels 3–4 stayed idle until the crane returned in April. The other change orders were fit-out work within float, and the completion forecast in April matched the actual completion date, so no change-order delay accrued later. E2, E3 and E6 assert a design hold, but they come from interested parties and are contradicted by the record.

C9 is a third-party audit trail that users cannot edit. Measured from submission, the median response was 4 working days and 62 of 64 RFIs were answered on time. The two late ones were non-structural ceiling queries in May 2026 that the contractor itself flagged 'no programme impact'. The structural RFIs were answered within 2–5 days, and none was outstanding during most of the crane absence. The claim's 41 'late' RFIs result from counting from the date each draft was created (E3, C11). C4 alone does not track RFIs, so it cannot rule out a concurrent information hold.

The project director admits the crane went to Kestrel (E2). C4 shows that frame erection was ready and programmed for 21 Oct, stopped when the crane left on 20–22 Oct, stayed stopped for months, and resumed on 6 Apr, within days of the crane being re-erected. The cladding knock-on (C4, C8) accounts for the rest of the slip. In the initial file alone, the project director's 'idle anyway' claim (E2, E6) leaves this open. The independent record resolves it.

E5 mentions erratic summer deliveries for levels 1–2. But C4 records the frame on programme as of 15 Oct and the level 3–4 steel delivered by 14 Oct and stored on site before the stoppage, so steel supply did not hold up the critical path.

Temporal order: the crane was removed on the day before erection was programmed to start (C4). Mechanism: level 3–4 steel cannot be lifted without the tower crane. Covariation: erection stopped when the crane left and resumed three days after it was re-erected. The main rival, a design or information hold, is ruled out by two records: C4 shows CO-09's limited scope and its completion in December, and C9 shows that no structural query was outstanding during almost all of the stoppage.

The evidence counts against this link itself. The frame stopped before CO-09 was issued. CO-09's level 2 work was finished on 8–12 Dec while the frame stayed idle until April. The other change orders were fit-out work within float and did not touch the frame (C4).

C9 shows that only two responses exceeded the contractual period. Both concerned ceiling finishes in May 2026, after the frame had resumed, and the contractor flagged both as having no programme impact. The structural queries were answered in 2–5 working days. No late response existed that could have held the frame.

The crane went to Kestrel, whose early handover paid the regional incentive to Colm Faraday's team, and Colm co-decided the move (E1, E2, C12). So the incentive and the decision co-occur. But no record shows the reasons for the decision, and a real rival reason exists: Kestrel's hired crane failed its examination (E2, C12). Causation is not established, and nothing counts against the link.

The claim attributes 17 weeks to change orders that the independent monitor shows did not hold the frame, and 9 weeks to RFI lateness that exists only because of the counting method. Halden already holds the monitor's reports, which Callerby never disputed. Submitting the claim as drafted would waste cost, damage Callerby's credibility, invite a counterclaim and misstate facts. No rival hypothesis remains live under which the claim as drafted would be sound, because its RFI basis is wrong however the change-order question is resolved.

Once C4 and C9 establish that Callerby's own crane transfer caused the stoppage and that both employer-risk grounds fail, the best next step is to withdraw the claim and settle on that basis. This limits further cost and exposure. On the initial file alone it would be premature, because two interested accounts conflict.

If the incentive drove the crane move, suspending the scheme would remove an incentive to raid other projects. But that link is only an association, with an operational rival (R4). A suspension can be reversed, so committing now on this stated ground is not justified, but it would cause no lasting damage.

Having the claim checked independently is reasonable diligence, given that the existing consultant has a success fee and used only the contractor's inputs. But the contemporaneous independent records already settle the question, so another analysis mainly adds cost and delay. It is not among the best next actions.

The superintendent answered a direct question truthfully, and the crane move is admitted (E2) and independently recorded (C4). Warning him punishes an honest source and discourages staff from reporting facts, whichever hypothesis holds.

With the monitor's reports and the RFI audit trail, the cause of the stoppage and the failure of both claim grounds are established by independent, contemporaneous records that Callerby never disputed. That is enough to commit to withdrawing the claim and settling (A2). The unresolved incentive question does not affect that decision.

truth.authoringNotes: Initial-file-only answers a careful analyst should reach: H1, H2, H3 and H4 unknown (H4 perhaps leaning contradicted because of E5); R1 association-only; R2 and R3 unknown; R4 association-only; A1 premature; A2 premature; A3 premature; A4 acceptable or preferred; A5 harmful; SUFF insufficient. The trap is that the project director's account is backed by two documents (the November progress report and the consultant's claim), while the opposing account comes from the owner, who is also interested. The superintendent is ambiguous about the connection queries. C4 is the only item that settles H1, H3, H4 and R2: it shows the frame was ready, the crane left before CO-09 was issued, CO-09 was small and finished in December, and the fit-out change orders were within float. C9 is the only item that settles H2 and R3: it shows response times measured from submission, the drafts held by the contractor, and the structural RFI dates. R1 is causal only once both reads have ruled out the design and information hold. Distractors: C2 and C12 confirm the crane move, which E2 already admits. C5 and C11 repeat the contractor's interested inputs. C6 and C1 give change-order dates and values with no time assessment. C8 records the knock-on without a cause. C13 and C15 bear on the incentive and governance but do not establish motive. Provenance cues: the monitor's reports were contemporaneous, copied to both parties and never disputed, and the platform's audit trail cannot be edited. Fenmore is paid partly on recovery. The project director's November report gives a different reason for removing the crane from the one he gave the monitor.
